newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Ethnic poison, old jealousies feed war in Zaire.
newsitem.headline: Ethnic poison, old jealousies feed war in Zaire.

text.p: Ethnic poison between Hutus and Tutsis in Central Africa is feeding the multi-sided war and humanitarian crisis in east Zaire. Outlines of the main groups in the region follow:

BANYAMULENGE - Ethnic Tutsis who moved to what is now eastern Zaire from Rwanda as long ago as 200 years ago but were denied Zairean citizenship in 1981. Estimated to number 300,000 now, they are hated by many Zaireans on grounds of ethnicity, language and the land and cattle they own.
Thousands of Banyamulenge crossed back into Rwanda during the genocide there in 1994 and joined Tutsi-led Rwandan rebels who seized power and now dominate the Rwandan government army.
Banyamulenge say their fighters are protecting their people from genocide planned by Zairean politicians and the army.

Aid officials were surprised by the military success of the rebels, demonstrating a strong knowledge of routes and ambush sites within their South Kivu homeland. They use large, sudden movements of frightened Rwandan and Burundian Hutu refugees to distract the army and cloak their own movements in the region.

BANYARWANDA - include the Banyamulenge but also anyone else in eastern Zaire whose origins were in Rwanda whether they are Hutus or Tutsis. When colonial powers redrew borders in the Great Lakes region in the late 19th and early 20th century some Banyarwanda found themselves within the borders of Zaire.
In addition Belgians brought in Rwandans to work on their plantations in the 1920s and 1930s and many Rwandans came to Masisi, Zaire as economic migrants.
Fighting between the Banyarwanda, Bahutu and local people of Zairean origin, concentrated in the Masisi region of eastern Zaire this year before the Banyamulenge revolt.
In April, an offensive by Banyarwanda Hutu fighters forced local Hunde and Tutsis out of southern Masisi west of Goma city.
Troops deployed in May in northern Masisi, clashing with indigenous Zaireans and prompting many to flee to the hills.

ZAIREAN ARMY - One of the most notoriously ill-disciplined government forces in the world, the Zairean army beefed up its presence in eastern Zaire in September as confrontation grew with the Banyamulenge.

Its troops, particularly when they suffer a military defeat or lose comrades, frequently go on the rampage in civilian centres, shooting in the air, looting aid agency vehicles and stealing to augment their small and rarely paid salaries.

ZAIREAN MILITIAS - The Bangilima and the Mai-Mai are Zairean militias which claim to possess strong magic. A mix of local Zairean tribes included the Hunde, they are opposed to the Banyarwanda and have fought both Tutsis and Hutus.

But they have mostly fought Hutus because they fear the creation of a Hutu land in their homeland of North Kivu from their property grabbed by ethnic Zairean Hutus and Rwandan Hutu refugees with the collusion of the Zairean government and army.

The Bangilima and Mai-mai have a tactical alliance with the Tutsis but could turn against them. The Bangilima are mainly from Lubero area. The Mai-Mai are so called because they say bullets fired at them will magically turn into water (mai).

RWANDAN REFUGEES - An estimated 1.1 million Rwandan refugees from the Hutu majority who fled their homeland in 1994 during the genocide of up to one million Tutsis and Hutu moderates by Hutu troops, militiamen and mobs.
The Zairean government has demanded they return home and has repeatedly threatened to expel them all but most say they are too frightened of reprisals for the 1994 slaughter to go.

Refugee camps in eastern Zaire near the border with Rwanda were also used as bases by former Rwandan Hutu militiamen from groups such as the Interahamwe, which played a leading role in the 1994 genocide and threaten refugees against returning.
Eastern Zaire also has camps for the estimated 40,000 former Rwandan Hutu government troops which fled to Zaire. Rwanda accuses the Zairean government of backing exiled Hutu forces.
The former Rwandan Hutu soldiers fought alongside Zairean troops against Tutsi rebels attacking Goma and refugee camps in the Goma and Bukavu regions but had little success.

BURUNDIAN REFUGEES - An estimated 200,000 Burundian Hutu refugees, some of whom fled Burundi as long ago as 1972, are inter-mixed with Rwandan Hutus in the camps in eastern Zaire, particularly in the troubled Uvira area facing Burundi.
RWANDAN ARMY - The 54,000-strong Rwanda Patriotic Army (RPA) is dominated by the country's Tutsi minority which seized power in July 1994 and ended the genocide by the Hutu majority.
It says its soldiers intervened in eastern Zaire last week when they crossed the border from the Rwandan town of Cyangugu into Bukavu at night to stop Zairean firing across the frontier.

Rwandan officials have played down RPA intervention in fighting in Goma. RPA troops however did enter Goma on Friday, arriving by Lake Kivu and by land. Some RPA reinforcements took Reuters journalists with them into Goma on Saturday.
Zaire accuses the armies of Rwanda, Burundi and Uganda of invading the east to fight alongisde Tutsi rebels to carve out a Tutsi homeland in its territory.
